sentences.text: The genus name means 'silver lizard' because it was discovered in Argentina, which literally translates to 'silver land'.
The animal is distinguished by a wide ridge on the medial side of the humerus, an extremely compressed midshaft, a subtriangular distal radius, and extremely elongated metacarpals.
Due to being known from few scattered bones, the morphology, size, and complete classification of Argyrosaurus are not well known.
One estimate suggested the creature weighed up to 12 tonnes.
In 2012, Thomas Holtz estimated Argyrosaurus could reach 28 meters in length and weigh between 43.5 and 50.8 tonnes.
A forelimb that likely belongs to this genus and a probable nest have been found in Entre Ríos Province.
The species Argyrosaurus superbus was formally described by Richard Lydekker in 1893 based on a complete forelimb found by Carlos Ameghino in the Chico River of Chubut.
The holotype of Argyrosaurus superbus is a massive left forelimb found at the Chico River in the Lago Colhué Huapi Formation.
The holotype forelimb was originally part of a complete skeleton, but the rest of the remains were destroyed during excavation.
In 1978, a commission from the National University of Tucumán found new remains along the Senguerr River in Santa Cruz Province.
Researchers suggest Argyrosaurus may be related to Alamosaurus.
Argyrosaurus is classified within the family Argyrosauridae.
In 2012, Argyrosaurus was placed in the family Argyrosauridae alongside the Egyptian genus Paralititan.
The time range for Argyrosaurus is from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
Fossils of Argyrosaurus have been found in the Bajo Barreal, Laguna Palacio, and Castillo formations in Argentina, and the Asencio Formation in Uruguay.
Recent studies suggest the area where the holotype was found dates to the early late Maastrichtian rather than the early Coniacian.
Argyrosaurus is estimated to have reached about 21 meters in length, though some estimates suggest it could have reached 30 meters.
In 2012, Philip Mannion and Alejandro Otero argued that only the holotype remains unambiguously belong to the genus Argyrosaurus.
Mannion and Otero considered the partial skeleton PLV 4628/MACN-CH 217 to be a distinct genus named Elaltitan.
